attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the tilemap to set the road tiles as walls so that the Player sprite appears to be driving on top of the road? Do not change any of the tiles along the bottom row!
steps.senseiHelp:
Solutions:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you add walls to tiles on the tilemap?

❓ How can you find the location of a tile on the tilemap?

❓ If the Player sprite has a vx value of 100 and a vy value of 0, what directions will it only be able to move in?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that they can edit the tilemap using the “Draw Walls'' and “Fill Tool” icons to add walls to tiles. If they are stuck, point out which tiles will act as the road for the Player sprite to drive on.

💡Make sure the Ninja uses the provided tilemap and only adds walls to the existing  road tiles. They should not add any other customizations to the tilemap; those can be added to the project once saved to My Stuff.

💡Encourage the ninja to connect the vx/vy values in the [move sprite with buttons] block to how they set a sprite’s velocity y in the previous activity. Remind the ninja that x values determine the left/right direction of a sprite, whereas y values determine the up/down direction.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by updating the tilemap, so that the Player sprite appears to be driving on the road!


Click the square in the [set tilemap to] block to edit the tilemap. In the tilemap editor, notice the road tiles, which have brown dirt on the bottom, green grass in the middle, and black road on the top. Turn each of these road tiles into walls by first selecting the “Draw Walls” icon, then the “Fill Tool” from the menu. Click “Done” to return to the project’s code.


In the Player sprite’s [place sprite on top of] block, update the row parameter, so that the Player sprite begins the project on top of the road tile in the bottom left corner. Then, click + on the [move sprite with buttons] block and change the vy parameter to 0, so that the Player sprite can only move left and right along the road tiles.


Click ▶ to move the car Player sprite horizontally along the road of the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓Did you replace the tilemap coordinates with the (value) block in the [place sprite on top of] and [set tile at] blocks ?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the project know how many and where to place each Enemy sprite?

❓ How do you think the Enemy sprites will act as obstacles for the Player sprite in this project? What else might act as an obstacle?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the sequence of the [for element] loop. In this example, for each orange spawn tile on the tilemap, the project will place a cone sprite on top of it and erase the orange spawn tile. Because the loop uses the array of all orange tiles, the project knows how many tiles are in the array and where they are each located on the tilemap.
steps.instructions:
Place Enemy sprites on the tilemap to act as obstacles for the Player sprite to avoid!


Drag a [for element] loop into the bottom of the [on start] container. Open Scene to use an (array of all tile locations) block as the (list) value. Select the orange tile from the dropdown menu. The orange tile is a spawn tile and is setting the place for Enemy sprites to be created.


Drag the Enemy sprite’s [set sprite to] block from the [on start] container into the [for element] loop. Then, open Scene and drag [place sprite on top of] and [set tile at] blocks into the loop. Select the Enemy sprite’s name, then replace the tilemap coordinates in both blocks with the (value) variable from the loop. Leave the tile blank in the [set tile at] block.


Click ▶ to see Enemy sprites appear on the road in various places on the tilemap where the orange spawn tiles once were!

steps.hints: ❓Did you open the tilemap editor, select the orange tile, and click the paint tool to add more spawn tiles?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Where should the orange spawn tiles/cone sprites be placed so that the Player sprite can avoid them as well as the brown pit tiles?

❓ Why would you not want to have too many obstacles in a row? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to think strategically about where to place the orange spawn tiles/cone sprites on the tilemap, making sure there aren’t too many in a row and/or they aren’t too close to the brown pit tiles. Prompt the ninja to think about how they can design the tilemap to be both challenging and fun for the user.
steps.instructions:
Edit the tilemap to add more obstacles for the Player sprite to avoid!


Click the square in the [set tilemap to] block to open the tilemap editor. Click “My Tiles” and select the orange tile. On top of the road tiles, replace a few railing tiles with an orange spawn tile.


Place them strategically so that the car sprite must avoid the spawned cone sprites and the brown pit tiles! Once finished, click “Done”. 


Click ▶ to see even more Enemy sprites appear on the road for the Player sprite to avoid!

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the Player sprite’s [vy (velocity y)] and  [ay (acceleration y)] so that it can “jump” when the A button is pressed, and then fall back to the ground?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the A button is pressed? Does the Player sprite move as you expected it would? 

❓ How does the Player sprite’s vy and ay values affect how it moves?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to test out the project to make sure that the values work correctly in the [set sprite vy (velocity y)] and [set sprite ay (acceleration y)] blocks. Prompt them to think about whether the game functions correctly with the placement of each obstacle and consider if they should change anything.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to be able to jump over both the Enemy sprites and the brown pit tiles!


Drag out an [on button pressed] container and place a [set sprite [x]] block inside of it. Select the Player sprite’s name, select [vy (velocity y)] from the dropdown menu, and type -200 into the parameter. This will enable the Player sprite to “jump”, by moving upwards on the screen when the A button is pressed. 


Code the Player sprite to come back down by adding another [set sprite [x]] block into the [on start] container, above the [for element] loop. Select the Player sprite’s name, select [ay (acceleration y)] from the dropdown menu, and type 500 into the parameter. This will create “gravity”, causing the Player sprite to fall back towards the road. 


Click ▶ to practice jumping over obstacles on the tilemap! Notice what happens when the A button is pressed multiple times.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add an [if then] conditional inside the [on button pressed] container so that the Player sprite can only jump when it’s touching a wall tile on the bottom?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Is the Player sprite able to jump while it’s in the air? Why or why not?

❓ Why would you want the Player sprite to only  jump when standing on a wall tile?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Prompt the ninja to think about what happens when they try to jump in the air—are they able to jump when not standing on a solid surface? Encourage the ninja to consider why they would want to add this realistic element to a game.
steps.instructions:
What happened when the A button was pressed repeatedly? The Player sprite stayed in the “air” for too long! 


Allow the Player sprite to jump only when it’s touching a wall tile on the bottom. Drag an [if then] conditional into the [on button pressed] container.


Open Scene and replace the <true> value with an <is sprite hitting wall> value block. Select [bottom] from the dropdown menu, then drag the [set sprite [vy (velocity y)]] block into the conditional.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite only be able to jump when it is touching the road wall tile on the bottom.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a [place sprite on top of] block in the [on sprite overlaps tile] container, so that the Player sprite resets to its starting position when it overlaps a brown pit tile?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓What happens when the Player sprite overlaps with a Enemy sprite? 

❓What happens when the Player sprite overlaps with a brown pit tile?

❓What type of effects might match what happens to the Player sprite on each of the overlap events?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to think about why they might not want the same action to happen when the Player sprite overlaps with different obstacles. Prompt the ninja to brainstorm how other obstacles or overlap events might be used differently in this project.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps with an obstacle!


Code the Player sprite to lose a life on overlap with an Enemy sprite by adding a [set life to] block into the [on start] container, below the [set tilemap to] block, and a [change life by] block into the [on (Player) overlaps (Enemy)] container, below the [destroy] block. 


Return the Player sprite to its starting position on overlap with a brown pit tile by duplicating its [place sprite on top of] block from the [on start] container, then placing it in the [on sprite overlaps tile] container with the brown pit tile selected.


Add a sound or visual effect when the Player sprite overlaps with an obstacle by adding a [play sound] or [camera shake] block into each of the overlap containers.


Click ▶ to try to move the Player sprite all the way to the finish line at the end of the tilemap, without overlapping an obstacle!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a [game over] block inside the [on sprite overlaps tile] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Does the game run as you expected it would? Is there anything you would change about the design of the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Once the ninja has moved the Player sprite all the way to the finish line tile, have them reflect on the mechanics of the game. Was it too easy or too hard? Were obstacles placed in appropriate places? Is there anything that might make the game more interesting?
steps.instructions:
End the game once the Player sprite has reached the finish line, without losing all of its lives!


Drag a [game over] block into the [on sprite overlaps tile] container with the finish line tile selected. Set the toggle to <WIN>, then add an effect with a [use effect] block.


Click ▶ to see the game end once the Player sprite has reached the finish line!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add customizations to your project, such as dialog boxes, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Make the project more engaging by adding directions with a dialog box and updating any sound or visual effects.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.title: Avoid the Roadblocks
subgroups.introduction: Create a 2D platformer project where the Player sprite moves horizontally across the screen, while jumping over obstacles.

validationItems.text: Set the tilemap walls. Set the Player sprite’s starting position, and set the Player sprite to only move left and right.
Spawn Enemy sprites to appear on the tilemap.
Add additional spawn tiles to the tilemap.
Player sprite jumps up when placed on a road tile and the A button is pressed.
Player sprite returns to starting position when it overlaps a hazard tile, and loses a life when it overlaps an Enemy sprite.
Game ends when the Player sprite overlaps the finish line tiles.
Game instructions are shared in a dialog box. Sound and visual effects are added to the game.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Green Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about 2D platformer games and physics. In 2D platformers, we see the game as if looking from the side. We can use physics concepts, like velocity and acceleration, to make our sprites jump up onto platforms and avoid obstacles. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:

badges.title: Let’s Get Physics-cal!
badges.description: Use physics to control sprite movement in a platformer-style tilemap project.

badges.title: Hop, Skip, and a Jump
badges.description: Set a sprite’s y-velocity (vy).

badges.title: Defying Gravity
badges.description: Set a sprite’s y-acceleration (ay).

badges.title: Wallflower
badges.description: Check if a sprite is touching a tilemap wall before making something happen in a project.
